 On October 26, Austria celebrates the National Day of the Republic of Austria—a day commemorating the restoration of the country’s independence after World War II and the declaration of permanent neutrality. It was on this day in 1955 that the Austrian Parliament passed the Neutrality Act, and since 1965, the date has been officially observed as a national holiday. In 2026, it falls on a Monday, and government agencies traditionally organize public events and tours for citizens. 
 The history of the Austrian National Holiday began after World War II. After the defeat of Nazi Germany, Austria came under the control of four Allied powers—the United States, the United Kingdom, France, and the Soviet Union. The country was divided into occupation zones, and Vienna was also under joint Allied control. Despite the restoration of democratic institutions, Austria was still unable to determine its political course entirely on its own. The situation changed only ten years after the end of the war, when the country signed the State Treaty and regained full sovereignty. 
 May 15, 1955, was a significant date. On that day, representatives of Austria and the four powers that had occupied it signed the State Treaty at the Belvedere Palace in Vienna. The document provided for the end of the occupation and the restoration of an independent Austrian state. The treaty entered into force on July 27, 1955, after which the withdrawal of foreign troops began. The last Allied troops left Austria by October 25. The following day, the country’s parliament passed a law on permanent neutrality—it was this event that later became the basis for the National Holiday. 
 Why is October 26 Celebrated? 
 On October 26, 1955, the Austrian National Council passed a constitutional law on neutrality. In it, the country declared its intention to maintain independence and not join any military alliances. This decision became an important symbol of an independent political course following years of occupation. Initially, the date was observed as Flag Day, and in 1965, it was officially renamed Austria’s National Holiday. Two years later, a separate law enshrined October 26 as a national holiday at the legislative level. Since then, this day has served as an annual reminder to Austrians of the restoration of sovereignty, national independence, and the country’s decision to adopt permanent neutrality. 
 It is important to distinguish between two events that are sometimes confused. The State Treaty was signed on May 15, 1955, and the law on neutrality was adopted on October 26 of the same year. It is the latter date that became a national holiday. Therefore, Austria celebrates not the day the document ending the occupation was signed, but the day its parliament enshrined the country’s political course following the restoration of independence. This distinction helps to better understand why the date is so significant for modern Austrian history. 
 What Does Austria’s Neutrality Mean? 
 The concept of neutrality has become one of the cornerstones of Austrian foreign policy. The 1955 law stipulates that the country will not join military alliances and will not allow other states to establish military bases on its territory. In this way, Austria sought to preserve its independence and avoid being drawn into one of the military blocs in the East-West confrontation during the Cold War. At the same time, neutrality does not mean that a state must cease diplomatic, cultural, or trade relations with other countries. It primarily concerns the military sphere and a state’s conduct during international armed conflicts. 
 Subsequently, Austria became a member of international organizations, notably the United Nations in 1955 and the European Union in 1995. Joining the EU did not abolish Austrian neutrality, but it did raise the question of how to reconcile it with international obligations and security cooperation. Therefore, neutrality remains a subject of political and public debate in the country. For many Austrians, it is still an important part of national identity, linked to the experience of war and the restoration of independence. At the same time, the specific application of neutrality depends on Austrian legislation, international agreements, and political decisions. 
 How Austrians Celebrate October 26 
 The national holiday is marked by official ceremonies, cultural events, and activities for the whole family. Red-white-red flags—in the colors of the Austrian national flag—are displayed throughout the country. In Vienna, one of the main venues for the celebrations is Heldenplatz, where the Austrian Armed Forces showcase their vehicles, equipment, and various areas of their work. There are also solemn ceremonies during which new recruits take their oaths. For visitors, this is an opportunity to see military equipment up close, learn more about the army’s work, and talk with service members. The program may vary from year to year, but it typically combines official ceremonies with public events. 
 Another notable tradition is the “open house” at government institutions. On Austria Day, citizens can visit the parliament, the Federal Chancellor’s Office, the President’s Office, and certain ministries. Guided tours are organized for visitors, during which they can see meeting halls, historic rooms, and areas not usually accessible to the general public. In Parliament, meetings with members of Parliament are held, information is provided about the work of the legislative body, and programs for children are organized. Such events not only allow people to celebrate the national holiday but also to better understand how Austria’s democratic institutions function. 
 The holiday isn’t limited to official events. Austria also hosts sporting events, including mass runs and walks, and federal museums may offer free admission or special visiting conditions. This provides an opportunity to spend the day actively, visit an exhibition, or learn about the country’s history. In some cities, concerts and other cultural events take place. For many families, October 26 is an opportunity to spend time together, visit interesting places, or go for a walk. Thus, the National Holiday has not only a political but also a social dimension: it brings together historical memory, culture, and recreation. 
 What Will Happen on October 26, 2026 
 In 2026, Austria’s National Holiday falls on Monday, October 26. On this day, the country’s parliament will traditionally hold an Open House: visitors will be able to see the chambers of the National Council and the Federal Council, the historic hall of the Federal Assembly, and areas that are usually closed to the public. According to the parliament, in 2026 it will be open to visitors from 10:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., with the last admission scheduled for approximately 2:00 p.m. Advance registration for specific time slots is required for tours to reduce lines. 
 A separate program is planned for Heldenplatz in Vienna. According to the Office of the Federal President, events will include a wreath-laying ceremony, a swearing-in ceremony for new members of parliament, and a televised address by the president to the public. Government agencies are also organizing tours and other events, though the exact schedule varies by location. Therefore, anyone planning to attend the celebrations should check the official websites in advance for details. 
 Interesting Facts About Austria’s National Holiday 
 The holiday was established ten years after the end of World War II. That is how long it took the country to regain full sovereignty following a period of occupation. 
 The State Treaty and the Neutrality Act are different documents. The former was signed on May 15, 1955, while the latter was passed by parliament on October 26. 
 Originally, it was Flag Day. The date was designated “Austria’s National Holiday” in 1965, and its status was later enshrined in a separate law. 
 Neutrality does not prohibit international relations. Austria may maintain diplomatic and economic ties with other countries, as well as participate in the work of international organizations. 
 The holiday provides access to government buildings. In Vienna, citizens can tour the parliament and government offices, which are not typically open to the public. 
 Austria’s national holiday is more than just a day off on the calendar. It serves as a reminder of the country’s journey from postwar occupation to the restoration of sovereignty, as well as the political decision that shaped its foreign policy for decades. Every year on October 26, Austrians honor this chapter of history, and public events give them the opportunity to become more familiar with state institutions. In 2026, the celebrations will once again combine official ceremonies, military parades, guided tours, and cultural events.
